headline: Senate panel urges VA study of medical cannabis as opioid alternative
dek: Senate Appropriations reports for FY2027 back VA cannabis and psychedelics research, fund hemp breeding and press the FDA on cannabinoid foods.
key_points: The Senate Appropriations Committee posted two FY2027 spending bills on 10 November with reports that touch cannabis, hemp and psychedelics.
The veterans report recommends a VA study of whether state medical cannabis programs are tied to lower opioid use and abuse among veterans.
The agriculture and FDA report funds hemp breeding and a federal hemp germplasm bank, but presses the FDA on food products that contain cannabinoids.
Report language guides agencies but is not law, and the stopgap funding that keeps the government open runs out on 11 December, the same day the federal hemp THC limits start.
body: The Senate Appropriations Committee has used next year's spending bills to tell federal agencies how to treat cannabis, hemp and psychedelics. On Tuesday, 10 November, the committee posted the text of its Fiscal Year 2027 bills for Military Construction and Veterans Affairs and for Agriculture and the FDA, together with the reports that explain them, according to Marijuana Moment.

The veterans report recommends that the Department of Veterans Affairs study whether state-approved medical cannabis programs, and veterans' access to them, are linked to a reduction in opioid use and abuse. The agriculture report funds hemp breeding and a national hemp germplasm repository. It also says the committee is concerned about food products that contain cannabinoids, and asks the FDA to report back on enforcement.
## What the veterans report asks for

The language on medical cannabis is short. The committee encourages the VA to consider clinical research on medical marijuana and recommends a study of the link between state medical cannabis programs, veterans' access to them and opioid outcomes. It is a recommendation, not a mandate, and it sets no deadline for the study.

The psychedelics section goes further. The report notes that the VA already supports psychedelic-assisted care research at its medical centres, including multisite clinical trials, and that it has formed an Integrated Project Team to plan for any treatments the FDA approves. It directs the VA Secretary to develop a plan to expand VA-led clinical and implementation research and to brief both appropriations committees on that plan within 180 days of the bill becoming law.

The report also reminds the VA of an earlier instruction, in Senate Report 119-43, to collect data for a five-year longitudinal study of veterans who receive these therapies. It encourages research on ibogaine and other psychedelic compounds for treatment-resistant post-traumatic stress disorder, and asks the VA to find a privacy-safe way to count, on a voluntary and de-identified basis, how many veterans travel abroad for treatments such as ibogaine that are not available in the United States.
> Congress is writing cannabis into the federal health system one report paragraph at a time, while the industry's big asks stay outside the bills.
## Hemp gets research money, and a warning

For hemp farmers, the agriculture report is the friendlier document. It tells the Agricultural Research Service to keep funding hemp genetics work at no less than the fiscal 2026 level, including breeding with new editing techniques, and directs ARS to establish and maintain a hemp germplasm repository at its Plant Genetics Resources Research Unit. The report recalls that the national hemp germplasm collection was destroyed in the 1980s, leaving breeders without a public seed bank, and encourages ARS to work with 1890 land-grant institutions that already run hemp programmes.

A third hemp section funds regional research on how to fit hemp into existing cropping, processing and marketing systems, again at no less than the fiscal 2026 level. The committee describes an emerging market for US hemp for a variety of uses.

The same report is less welcoming to the products that drove the hemp boom. Marijuana Moment reports that the committee says it remains concerned by the growth of food products containing cannabinoids, because no cannabinoid is approved as a food additive, and asks the FDA to report within 90 days of enactment on its enforcement against unlawful products. Elsewhere it urges the FDA to improve data-sharing with state regulators, including through the agency's information-sharing agreement on cannabinoid hemp products.
## Pain and psychedelics at the FDA

In a section on chronic pain, the agriculture report points to the FDA's draft guidance on developing non-opioid analgesics and cites research on botanical and cannabinoid-based therapies. It also encourages the FDA to work with the VA, the Defense Department and the National Institutes of Health on clinical trials of MDMA, psilocybin, ibogaine and 5-MeO-DMT, and on public-private research partnerships, with an update due within 180 days of enactment.

None of this changes cannabis's legal status. Report language tells agencies what Congress expects; it does not amend the Controlled Substances Act, and it runs separately from the administration's rescheduling process.
## Why the timing matters

The reports are a statement of intent for bills that have not passed. Congress enacted no regular FY2027 spending bills before the fiscal year began on 1 October. Instead, the Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2027, signed on 2 September, funds the VA and other agencies through 11 December 2026, according to the Congressional Research Service. The House passed its own version of the veterans spending bill, H.R. 8469, on 15 May.

That date is doing double duty. The same stopgap law pushed most of the new federal hemp definition, which bars products with more than 0.4 milligrams of total THC per container, back to 11 December. As we reported on 12 November, the Senate's agriculture bill funds hemp programmes but keeps that THC cap in place. So Congress's next funding deadline and the hemp industry's deadline land on the same day, and whatever vehicle Congress uses to keep the government open is also the most likely place for any hemp change.

For medical cannabis operators, a VA study would be a slow-moving but significant signal. Veterans are a large share of medical patients in many state programmes, and a federal study tying state access to lower opioid harm would add weight to arguments for broader federal recognition. For hemp food and drink makers, the 90-day FDA report request points the other way: more federal attention on enforcement, not less.
## What to watch

The first marker is 11 December, when the stopgap funding and most federal hemp THC restrictions both expire or take effect unless Congress acts. Watch whether the Senate's report language survives negotiations with the House into a final FY2027 package, and whether any short-term funding bill carries a hemp delay. If the bills become law, the clocks start: 90 days for the FDA's cannabinoid food enforcement report, and 180 days for the VA psychedelics briefing and the FDA psychedelics research update.
